chunk_findings.detail:
`_parse_lines(chunk: bytes)` iterates the chunk's byte lines (`for raw in chunk.split(b"\n"):`; splitting a `bytes` chunk requires a bytes separator), and the unchanged `line = raw.strip()` therefore yields `bytes`. The new helper then searches that value with a `str` literal:

    _LINE_START = '{"agent":'          # str
    ...
    at = line.find(_LINE_START, 1)     # line is bytes

`bytes.find` with a `str` argument raises `TypeError: argument should be integer or bytes-like object, not 'str'`, and `_parse_lines` does not wrap the `_recover_glued` call in any `try`. Concrete input: the exact torn-tail case the change is meant to fix — a shard ending in an unterminated fragment, e.g. file bytes `b'{"agent":"a","body":"x'` (no trailing `\n`), then the fixed writer appends the next event. On read, `chunk.split(b"\n")` yields the fragment as a non-empty `bytes` line; `_parse_event` returns `None` (the `JSONDecodeError`/`UnicodeDecodeError` from a torn/invalid fragment are `ValueError`s, which is exactly why they are caught), so `_parse_lines` immediately calls `_recover_glued(fragment_bytes)` and raises `TypeError` before any recovery can happen. The exception propagates out of `read_all` instead of yielding the fragment as a skipped line plus the recovered/appended event, so every shard with a torn tail (and every other unparseable line) becomes a hard read failure. The helpers' own annotations (`_parse_event(line: str)`, `_recover_glued(line: str)`) expose the bytes/str mismatch: the parsing pipeline works on bytes, the `_LINE_START` literal is a `str`, and the find on line 1 of `_recover_glued` cannot succeed.

chunk_findings.detail: The patch bumps `_code_fingerprint` by adding `_parse_lines`, `_parse_event` and `_recover_glued` to the tuple of functions it hashes. That fingerprint is the version stamped into an event's identity: it is computed over exactly the functions that produce a stored id (`Event.from_json`, `Event.compute_id`, `Event.body`, `canonical`), i.e. `compute_id()` is not a pure hash of the body but of the body plus this code fingerprint. The same patch then gates the new reader-side recovery on `ev.id == ev.compute_id()` (in `_recover_glued`). Those two halves contradict each other for precisely the data the fix exists to repair: the glued events it must recover were written by the *older* writer, so their stored `id` was computed under the *old* fingerprint, while `_recover_glued` recomputes it under the new one. Concretely, for a pre-change shard whose last line is `b'{"agent":"old","bo{"agent":"after","body":"after","id":"<id derived under the old fingerprint>","ts":...}\n'`, `_parse_event` returns `None`, `_recover_glued` finds the second `{"agent":` and parses the event correctly, but `ev.id != ev.compute_id()` (fingerprint now differs), so it returns `None` and read_all still drops `after`. The regression that “closes” this bug only passes because its glued fixture is manufactured with the *current* code's `compute_id()`, so the old-vs-new fingerprint mismatch is never exercised; on real, already-corrupted shards the fix is a no-op.

chunk_findings.detail: `ensure()` wraps the *second* staleness check (and `_rebuild_locked`) in `try: ... except (TimeoutError, OSError, sqlite3.Error)`, i.e. the code explicitly anticipates that `stale()` can raise a `sqlite3.Error`. The *first* `stale()` call, however, happens one line above the `try:` and is not guarded at all, so an unreadable/incomplete index still produces a traceback on the read path — exactly the symptom the change claims to remove ("A READ path, so it never fails for the index's sake … the state still comes from the log"). Concrete input: the race described in Bcdfb199cc0 can publish a half-built `index.db` (that is precisely how the report's `sqlite3.OperationalError: no such table: meta` arises), and any pre-existing corrupt/truncated/foreign file at `self.path` does the same. With a schema-less `index.db` beside a log containing one `task.added` event, `Store(repo, cfg).ensure(log)` calls `self.stale(log)`, which queries `meta` and raises `sqlite3.OperationalError`; because this call is outside the `try`, `ensure()` propagates it instead of falling back to `fold(log.read_all(), strict=False)`, and `ddflow similar` exits 1 — while the equivalent inner call would have been swallowed by the handler. Moving the initial `stale()` into the guarded block (or treating any `stale()` failure as "stale") is needed for the stated intent to hold.

chunk_findings.detail: `ensure`'s docstring promises the read path "never fails for the index's sake", and the new `try/except (TimeoutError, OSError, sqlite3.Error)` implements that — but only for everything *after* the very first statement. The initial `if not self.stale(log):` sits outside the guard. Deciding staleness means consulting the index itself (that is how the index records how far it has folded the log), so any SQLite failure while reading `index.db` there escapes `ensure` unchanged. The bug being fixed already demonstrates the input: the probe reports `sqlite3.OperationalError: no such table: meta` on the shared half-built file, i.e. an `index.db` left partially written by the unfixed race (or truncated by a crash/ENOSPC). With such a file present, `ensure(log)` raises that same `sqlite3.OperationalError` at the first line, before the lock or the fallback is ever reached, so `ddflow similar` still tracebacks with exit 1 — exactly the symptom Bcdfb199cc0 is supposed to remove, and the test `test_ensure_does_not_traceback_when_the_rebuild_cannot_run` does not catch it because it monkeypatches `_rebuild_locked` and never makes `stale` fail. The fallback needs to wrap the initial staleness check too (or `stale` must treat an unreadable index as stale).

chunk_findings.detail:
The new race guard is gated on `finding.id`, justified by the comment that "`auto_id` is time-salted" so an unnamed id cannot collide. But the id is produced by `auto_id("R", finding.question, finding.claim)` (visible in the hunk at `rid = finding.id or auto_id("R", ...)`) — i.e. it is derived from the note's content, so two adds of the same question/claim produce the *same* `rid`. The docstring's own promise ("The same record again is idempotent") only makes sense under that deterministic behavior, and the pre-lock `_research_id_taken` call is applied unconditionally (not just for `finding.id`), which would be pointless if auto ids never collided.

Interleaving that defeats the fix: two agents concurrently run `research add` with no `--id` and the same question/claim (different verdict text), so both compute `rid = R…`. Both `_load` before either appends, so both pre-lock `_research_id_taken` calls return `None`; both `check_add` calls see the id as free. They then serialize on `log.transaction()`. The first appends `research.recorded` for `R…`. The second acquires the lock but skips the under-lock re-fold because `finding.id` is falsy, appends the same `rid`, and the fold replaces the first record — the exact silent overwrite of question/claim/verdict that B14d796e03b is supposed to close. The pre-lock check only closes the sequential case; the concurrent case is explicitly excluded by the `if finding.id:` guard.

Secondary consequence of the same wrong assumption: for a deterministic auto id, the guidance in the refusal message ("To file a separate finding: another `--id`, or none for a generated one") is a loop — omitting `--id` regenerates the very `rid` just reported as taken.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_cannot_write` compares the captured error code against the module constant `sqlite3.SQLITE_CANTOPEN`:

```python
getattr(exc, "sqlite_errorcode", None) == sqlite3.SQLITE_CANTOPEN
```

CPython's `sqlite3` module does not expose SQLITE result-code constants; the only `SQLITE_*` names it defines are `SQLITE_OK`, `SQLITE_DENY`, and `SQLITE_IGNORE` (the authorizer codes). `sqlite_errorcode`/`sqlite_errorname` were added as *exception attributes*, but no `SQLITE_CANTOPEN` module attribute came with them — which is why the conventional workaround is to hard-code `14`. Consequently the right-hand operand raises `AttributeError: module 'sqlite3' has no attribute 'SQLITE_CANTOPEN'` the moment `_cannot_write` is evaluated.

This is reached whenever `ensure` catches a `TimeoutError`/`OSError`/`sqlite3.OperationalError` for which `_environmental(exc)` is `False` — i.e. precisely the "cannot open the database file" case this helper was written for. Concrete demonstration: make the index directory unwritable (`chmod a-w .ddflow`) or run with a full/read-only filesystem; `ddflow similar` on a stale index calls `ensure` → `_rebuild` → `sqlite3.connect(tmp)` fails with `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file` (code 14) → `_environmental` is false → `_cannot_write(exc)` is called → `AttributeError` is raised inside the `except` handler, is not in the caught tuple, and propagates. So a read path tracebacks (exit 1) instead of degrading to `fold(log.read_all(), strict=False)` — exactly the failure mode the docstring promises to eliminate ("A READ path, so it never fails for the index's sake"). The check should use the raw integer (`14` / `SQLITE_CANTOPEN`) or `exc.sqlite_errorname == "SQLITE_CANTOPEN"`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new temp name is deliberately made unguessable (`{name}-rebuilding.{pid}.{token}`) with the stated rationale that "a temp file that nothing else can name cannot be unlinked or published by anything else." But the immediately preceding line unconditionally unlinks every file matching `self.path.parent.glob(f"{self.path.name}-rebuilding*")`, which is precisely the pattern of those new temp files. The only protection is the advisory lock ("Under the lock no other rebuild of THIS version is running"), yet the comment two lines later admits "the lock is advisory." In any environment where the advisory lock does not serialize the two processes (e.g. the index on an NFS/CIFS mount, or a lock implementation that silently no-ops), process B's cleanup deletes process A's live `index.db-rebuilding.<pid>.<token>` file while A is still building, so A's publish (`tmp.replace(self.path)`) raises `FileNotFoundError` — the identical symptom of bug Bcdfb199cc0, now merely under a different filename. Because the glob is age-ungated (unlike the legacy branch, which correctly uses `LEGACY_TEMP_MAX_AGE_S`), it will happily delete a temp that was created milliseconds ago; gating it by age (or not globbing the new scheme at all, since the lock is supposed to be the sole owner) would remove the contradiction.

chunk_findings.detail: The test is named for the verdict field and is the only test that tries to pin down that a *verdict-only* difference under a taken id must be refused, but the second add (line 36) does not change only the verdict: it also sets `probe="p"` while the first add (line 35) leaves `probe` at its default `None`. The verdict field is therefore never isolated. Concretely, if the fix's payload-and-equality key (`_research_fields`) omitted `verdict` — the exact field the bug report calls out ("overwrites question, claim and verdict") — the second add would still be refused because `probe` differs, so `out.exit == REFUSED` holds and the test passes on the buggy behaviour. The guard tests do not close the hole: `test_every_recorded_field_is_a_note_attribute` only asserts `set(_research_fields(...)) <= ResearchNote` field names (a missing key is allowed), and `test_every_recorded_field_round_trips_through_the_fold` iterates over the keys `_research_fields` returns, so a dropped `verdict` is simply never examined. Given an implementation whose duplicate/idempotence key excludes `verdict`, a re-add that changes only the verdict is either silently ignored (reported `unchanged`) or not refused, and no test in this file fails. Compare with the question/claim case: test 1 changes question and claim together and does catch those omissions; verdict is the one field from the bug report without an isolating regression case. The fix is to make the second add identical to the first except `verdict` (and drop the `probe` change, or add a separate verdict-only test).

chunk_findings.detail:
`_cannot_write` compares the captured error code against the module constant `sqlite3.SQLITE_CANTOPEN`:

```python
getattr(exc, "sqlite_errorcode", None) == sqlite3.SQLITE_CANTOPEN
```

CPython's `sqlite3` module does not expose SQLITE result-code constants; the only `SQLITE_*` names it defines are `SQLITE_OK`, `SQLITE_DENY`, and `SQLITE_IGNORE` (the authorizer codes). `sqlite_errorcode`/`sqlite_errorname` were added as *exception attributes*, but no `SQLITE_CANTOPEN` module attribute came with them — which is why the conventional workaround is to hard-code `14`. Consequently the right-hand operand raises `AttributeError: module 'sqlite3' has no attribute 'SQLITE_CANTOPEN'` the moment `_cannot_write` is evaluated.

This is reached whenever `ensure` catches a `TimeoutError`/`OSError`/`sqlite3.OperationalError` for which `_environmental(exc)` is `False` — i.e. precisely the "cannot open the database file" case this helper was written for. Concrete demonstration: make the index directory unwritable (`chmod a-w .ddflow`) or run with a full/read-only filesystem; `ddflow similar` on a stale index calls `ensure` → `_rebuild` → `sqlite3.connect(tmp)` fails with `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file` (code 14) → `_environmental` is false → `_cannot_write(exc)` is called → `AttributeError` is raised inside the `except` handler, is not in the caught tuple, and propagates. So a read path tracebacks (exit 1) instead of degrading to `fold(log.read_all(), strict=False)` — exactly the failure mode the docstring promises to eliminate ("A READ path, so it never fails for the index's sake"). The check should use the raw integer (`14` / `SQLITE_CANTOPEN`) or `exc.sqlite_errorname == "SQLITE_CANTOPEN"`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_cannot_write` tests `getattr(exc, "sqlite_errorcode", None) == sqlite3.SQLITE_CANTOPEN`. The stdlib `sqlite3` module does not expose error-code constants; the only constants it defines are the authorizer ones (`SQLITE_OK`, `SQLITE_DENY`, `SQLITE_IGNORE`, `SQLITE_CREATE_INDEX`, …). So `sqlite3.SQLITE_CANTOPEN` raises `AttributeError` the moment this line executes. This line is exactly the path it was written for: on a read-only index directory `_build_into` raises `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file`; `ensure`'s `except (TimeoutError, OSError, sqlite3.OperationalError)` catches it, `_environmental(exc)` is False (that is why `_cannot_write` exists), so `self._cannot_write(exc)` is evaluated and blows up with `AttributeError: module 'sqlite3' has no attribute 'SQLITE_CANTOPEN'`. The `AttributeError` is not in the caught tuple, so it propagates out of `ensure` — turning the "unwritable directory degrades to the log" contract (documented in the `ensure` docstring) back into a traceback on the read path, i.e. the very failure this change claims to fix. Even if the constant did exist, comparing it to the extended `sqlite_errorcode` that SQLite normally reports for CANTOPEN would be broken, but the AttributeError is the concrete failure.
